projectTitle: Jaxonomy: JAX-native simulation engine for hybrid dynamical systems
description: Python library for modeling and simulating hybrid dynamical systems on JAX: block-diagram composition, ODE/DAE solvers, zero-crossing events, state machines, acausal multi-physics (electrical, mechanical, thermal, hydraulic), LQR/MPC/PID and Kalman/EKF/UKF control blocks, reduced-order modeling, FMI 2.0 co-simulation, and end-to-end automatic differentiation (jax.grad / vmap / jit) through the whole simulation.
rules: Jaxonomy is a simulation engine, unrelated to taxonomy/classification libraries with similar names. Import it as `import jaxonomy as jx`.

The standard flow is: `builder = jx.DiagramBuilder()`, `handle = builder.add(block)`, `builder.connect(src.output_ports[i], dst.input_ports[j])`, `diagram = builder.build()`, `context = diagram.create_context()`, `results = jx.simulate(diagram, context, stop_time=...)`.

`jx.simulate` takes `context` as a required positional argument (there is no context-less shortcut), and `options` must be a `SimulatorOptions` instance, not a dict. Read results via `results.time` and `results.outputs[name]`.

Do NOT use Jaxonomy to solve a plain ODE with no block-diagram composition, events, or hybrid dynamics — use Diffrax directly. Do NOT use it for robots with joints, actuators, contacts, or kinematic chains — that is Jaxterity, a separate library built on top of Jaxonomy. Do NOT use it for embedded code generation or cross-compilation — that is Jaxility.

The `Context` is an immutable carrier of state and parameters. Thread it through; never mutate it in place. State is NamedTuple-shaped, so read state out of the results or context rather than assigning into it.

Everything is differentiable by default: parameter estimation, trajectory optimization, and controller tuning are ordinary `jax.grad` optimizations over a `simulate` call. Avoid constructs that break gradients, such as Python-side branching on traced values or in-place mutation.

Parameter sweeps re-JIT per value: calling `diagram.with_parameter('p', float(v))` inside a Python loop keys the trace cache on the concrete value and recompiles every iteration. Wrap the scalar as `jnp.asarray(v)`, or use `simulate_batch` / `jax.vmap` from the start.

Update nested sub-system parameters by dot-path on the OUTER diagram: `outer.with_parameters({'inner.gain.gain': jnp.array(5.0)})`. Do not reach into `outer['inner']` — you will get a stale outer diagram. The dot-path form also composes under `vmap`.
`declare_periodic_update` requires an explicit `offset=0.0`; omitting it constructs successfully but crashes at the first step inside the scheduler.
To guard host-side checks in traced code use `isinstance(x, jax.core.Tracer)`, NOT `jax.core.is_concrete` — the latter is True under `jax.grad`'s tracer and silently breaks gradients.

Prefer the standard library blocks under `jx.library` (sources, math_ops, logic, routing, dynamics, nonlinearities, tables) over hand-rolling. Controls and estimation — LQR, MPC, PID, Kalman/EKF/UKF — are library blocks too.

For stiff systems with coupled fast and slow dynamics, set `ode_solver_method='bdf'`; the explicit default collapses its step size. For long or multi-rate runs, raise `SimulatorOptions(buffer_length=...)` or the recorder silently decimates the recording.

Inside model code, numeric operations go through the `npa` backend abstraction rather than `jnp` directly — this is a load-bearing invariant when authoring library-style blocks or custom `LeafSystem` subclasses.
`LookupTable1d.interp_1d` takes `method=`, not `mode=` (other blocks such as `Quantizer` and `Saturate` use `mode=`). `Saturate(limit=L)` is shorthand for symmetric `upper_limit=+L, lower_limit=-L`.
Prefer the notebooks under `docs/examples/` and the API reference at https://py.jaxonomy.com over guessing a signature.
